      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-07-07T23:09:07.271Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_the-protection-of-coromandel-brown-kiwi-has-activity-7480397517747265536-wjns","text":"The protection of Coromandel brown kiwi has received a boost with two years of council funding going to conservation group Project Kiwi Trust.

The trust will receive almost $40,000 from Waikato Regional Council’s Environmental Initiatives Fund for the purchase of predator control materials and track maintenance. This represents part of almost $480,000 in grants made to 15 projects announced in the 2025 funding round.

Established in 1996, Project Kiwi Trust works to protect Coromandel brown kiwi on the Kūaotunu Peninsula near Whitianga. For the kiwi population in the area to be stable and experience growth, pest and predator control needs to be maintained.The trust services and checks over 500 traps targeting mustelids throughout the year. They also support a bait station programme that targets rats and possums over some 70ha.

Since 2003, the trust has run a regular kiwi survey. Currently done every two years, the survey sees volunteers deployed to nine base sites over three nights. During a two-hour period each night, they record details about all the bird calls they hear and their location, along with other information such as atmospheric conditions.

Kiwi are also fitted with transmitters, so even though they may not call during the survey, it’s possible to detect them. An additional 17 sites allow for mapping of population change out of the core areas where kiwi have spread. The survey of base sites points to a growing kiwi population estimated at some 300 pairs, plus 150 juveniles and 150 chicks.

Read the full story here: https://bit.ly/4vx0xfu","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_the-protection-of-coromandel-brown-kiwi-has-activity-7480397517747265536-wjns"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-07-07T23:06:56.958Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_have-you-thought-about-pole-planting-to-help-activity-7480396971174834176-p3VQ","text":"Have you thought about pole planting to help erosion control? 

Poplar and willow are ideal to plant on erosion prone hillsides as their extensive root systems bind and hold the soil in place.

Heard that poplar and willow can be a pest? 

There’re a few things to consider. 

Many poplar and willow species and cultivars that were used historically performed well for soil conservation and served their purpose at the time.

However, ongoing research and development have produced improved, smaller-growing varieties with greater resilience, better pest and disease resistance, and fewer management challenges.

Earlier varieties were often more susceptible to disease, more palatable to pests such as possums, tended to grow very large, and were prone to spreading beyond intended areas—via broken branches and twigs (e.g. crack willow), root suckering (e.g. silver poplar), or seeding (particularly female willow varieties).

But today it is possible to select from a short list of varieties with low susceptibility to these problems. 

Purchasing poplar or willow poles, or rooted cuttings from a nursery is recommended to ensure you are purchasing non-invasive varieties that have been specially bred for soil conservation. 

You can find a guide to planting poplar and willow on your property here: https://bit.ly/4eAiiVj

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with MPI and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_have-you-thought-about-pole-planting-to-help-activity-7480396971174834176-p3VQ"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-07-01T22:09:02.872Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_we-spy-a-little-inanga-egg-or-two-activity-7478208072658792448-HBQc","text":"We spy a little inanga egg (or two)... 

Our freshwater ecologists in Integrated Catchment Management have been busy undertaking inanga spawning surveys in a tributary of the lower Waikato River. 

While searching monthly from March through to May, they observed an increase in egg density and nest abundances later in the season, along with a greater spatial extent at the site in Port Waikato. This included over 170 eggs in the biggest nest! 

This serves as a good reminder that undertaking multiple surveys across a season is extremely valuable, enabling better management of this newly threatened species within this area. The species has moved from At Risk – Declining to Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable under the Department of Conservations threat classification system. This change is linked to the scarcity of suitable spawning habitat nationwide.

Inanga are native to New Zealand and are the dominant species in the whitebait fishery. They are generally found in lowland systems in the Waikato, as they are poor swimmers and climbers. During the autumn, inanga move downstream to a location called the salt wedge, to catch the new and full moons and the associated spring tides. 

At this time, bankside vegetation is submerged and the inanga spawn hundreds to thousands of eggs amongst it. The eggs develop in the humid air and hatch when they become inundated by the next spring tide in the cycle. The hatchlings are swept to sea where they grow for approximately 20 weeks before returning as whitebait back into our freshwaters.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_we-spy-a-little-inanga-egg-or-two-activity-7478208072658792448-HBQc"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-29T22:15:02.510Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_its-three-years-on-from-the-discovery-of-activity-7477484805396410368-0v4Z","text":"It's three years on from the discovery of invasive freshwater clams in Lake Karāpiro, and we're still learning how these tiny hitchhikers operate in our awa (river). 

Researchers are working to understand how the clams move throughout the Waikato River, and what kind of tools we can use to manage the spread. But science isn't the whole story - everyday actions and education plays an important role too. 

Learn about how we're collaborating within the Waikato and beyond to stop the spread: https://bit.ly/3R5NaUw","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_its-three-years-on-from-the-discovery-of-activity-7477484805396410368-0v4Z"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-25T22:04:08.394Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_have-you-considered-pole-planting-this-winter-activity-7476032510318063616-3Sdi","text":"Have you considered pole planting this winter to help erosion control?

The benefits of planting poplar and willows include:

✅ Root systems which bind more soil than any other tree used on farms
✅ Once established they can reduce slips on hill country by 95%
✅ Sterilised willow also provide significant benefits to river management reducing the erosion of river and stream banks
✅ Well managed space planted poplars and willows allow ~ 90% of pasture growth
✅ Stock utilise their summer shade, and benefit from the shelter
✅ Both species are valuable sources of stock fodder during summer and drought conditions, and pollarding (removing/pruning upper limbs for fodder) helps maintain the canopy while extending the useful life of the trees.
✅ They absorb nutrients, particularly nitrogen from groundwater at deeper levels than pasture and absorb CO2, moderate the temperature and moisture microclimate
✅ They can be managed for timber and wood products and can be tanalised for farm posts, battens and rails 
✅ Increasing farm resilience to severe weather events.

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with MPI and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_have-you-considered-pole-planting-this-winter-activity-7476032510318063616-3Sdi"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-25T02:38:39.291Z","headline":"","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_heres-warren-maher-chair-of-waikato-regional-activity-7475739206334689280-u1Da","text":"Here's Warren Maher, chair of Waikato Regional Council, providing a wrap-up of today's full council meeting. 

Remember, our meetings are livestreamed and recorded so you can follow the discussion and decision making.

You can find them on our YouTube channel here: https://lnkd.in/gQBjkEUF","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_heres-warren-maher-chair-of-waikato-regional-activity-7475739206334689280-u1Da"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-21T23:30:03.264Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_do-you-work-with-a-community-biodiversity-activity-7474604579922354176-D0A4","text":"Do you work with a community biodiversity project in the Waikato region? 

We are currently piloting Kete Taiao Waikato, a new spatial data management tool designed to support community-led biodiversity projects, and we’d love your help. 

Kete Taiao Waikato can be used on desktop or mobile to record things like planting, pest control (animals and plants), monitoring and volunteer hours, all in one place. 

It works in the field and makes it easier to plan activities, track progress, and report on what’s being achieved. 

You can watch a short demo here: https://bit.ly/4vGljc0 

We're looking for groups who are:

✅ comfortable using technology (or keen to learn)

✅ willing to actively use the tool and provide feedback

✅ able to put some time into learning and using the system as part of their project work

✅ positive about helping test the tool so it works well for community groups.

If you're interested in being a pilot group for Kete Taiao Waikato, our biodiversity team would like to hear from you. Please email them directly including your group name, a contact person, and a short description of your project to ketetaiao@waikatoregion.govt.nz.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_do-you-work-with-a-community-biodiversity-activity-7474604579922354176-D0A4"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-18T23:03:25.753Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_waikato-regional-councils-pathways-to-the-activity-7473510715866292224-1wtL","text":"Waikato Regional Council’s Pathways to the Sea strategy won the Supreme Award at the 2026 LGFA Taituarā Local Government Excellence Awards last night, after winning the category for Excellence in Environmental Leadership.

The LGFA Taituarā Local Government Excellence Awards recognise excellence in local government management across a range of programmes and projects.

There were seven categories and 69 entries in total, a record-breaking number of entries celebrating the innovation, leadership and collaboration happening across local government in Aotearoa.

The panel of judges said that Pathways to the Sea "successfully reconciles legacy asset management decisions with today’s environmental and ecological expectations. 

"It is an exemplar in its use of new technology, a meticulous compilation of an evidence base over six years, its successful collaboration with 14 funding partners, and its partnership with iwi. The high level of national and international interest in this project makes this one of the year’s most transferable entries.”

Chief Executive Chris McLay, Senior Freshwater Ecologist Alicia Williams and Reliability Engineer Steve Hall collected the awards on behalf of the council at the ceremony at Tākina Wellington Convention and Exhibition Centre.

Senior Freshwater Ecologist Alicia Williams Alicia says Pathways to the Sea was a real passion project for everyone involved.

“Developing this strategy to provide safe downstream passage for tuna (eels) and other native fish through our flood protection infrastructure was something we deeply believed in, and we’re incredibly proud of the positive environmental outcomes it will deliver. 

“Winning this award wouldn’t have been possible without the support of our 14 funding partners, and our iwi and hapū partners across the Waikato.”

Learn more: https://lnkd.in/eaqcg32p ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_waikato-regional-councils-pathways-to-the-activity-7473510715866292224-1wtL"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-12T03:27:23.320Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_poplar-and-willow-planting-activity-7471040428352442368-U33T","text":"Have you considered pole planting to help erosion control? 

While some highly erosion-prone areas are best retired and planted in natives, others can be managed with pole planting to reduce erosion risk while still supporting productive pasture grazing.

Poplars and willows are valuable assets for any farm, offering strong root systems that contribute to soil retention and the protection of slopes, gullies, streams, and rivers. 

Once established, they can reduce hill country slips by up to 95%, significantly improving land stability. Sterilised willow species also play a crucial role in effective river management by minimizing erosion and helping maintain river channels. 

With thoughtful planting and management, poplars and willows support approximately 90% of pasture growth, ensuring ample grazing for livestock, which also benefit from increased shade and shelter during warmer months. 

Both species are valuable sources of stock fodder during summer and drought conditions, and pollarding (removing/pruning upper limbs for fodder) helps maintain the canopy while extending the useful life of the trees.

Additionally, these trees improve the farm environment by absorbing nutrients from deeper soil layers, particularly nitrogen, and sequestering CO2, resulting in a more resilient microclimate. 

For those interested in timber or wood products, poplars and willows can be managed for farm posts, battens, and rails when treated. 

Collectively, these benefits enhance overall farm resilience, particularly in the face of severe weather conditions.

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_poplar-and-willow-planting-activity-7471040428352442368-U33T"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil"},"datePublished":"2026-06-10T06:48:47.357Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_just-as-it-is-for-many-others-in-the-ag-and-activity-7470366336741814272-ew75","text":"Just as it is for many others in the ag and hospitality sectors, Fieldays is a big deal for us at Waikato Regional Council. 

Months of thinking, planning and organising goes into bringing our site together, with our Communications and Marketing section working closely with teams across our organisation to create a space where landowners, farmers, growers, residents and ratepayers, and industry stakeholders can have meaningful conversations with our people. 

This year our site design brings in two key themes: Our strategic direction and the importance of resilience in the Waikato region.

Taken from Te Pae Tawhiti | Strategic Direction 2026-2036, our map wall celebrates our diverse regional economy spanning agriculture, advanced manufacturing, technology, renewable energy, aquaculture, tourism, healthcare and forestry. You can read our strategic direction here: https://bit.ly/43k4esu

Building resilience is part of our council’s everyday activities, with environmental, scientific, policy and technical experts working every day managing flood protection infrastructure, generating and making sense of up-to-date data information, protecting and restoring environmental resources, planning transport networks, and so much more. 

We gathered a few of them to share their stories about some of the mahi (work) we are carrying out to support the region and its resilience. You can read them here: https://bit.ly/3QfLebs

So, if you’re heading out to Fieldays this week, stop by for a chat. We’ll be at our usual spot inside The Pavilion, site PE 36, with subject-matter experts available to answer your questions.

🔹 Our Primary Industry Engagement team will be on site throughout the week to talk about a range of issues relevant to rural audiences, including farm environment planning.
🔹 Our plant and animal pest team will be there to chat about species you need to look out for as well as tools, tips and support to control pest species around your property.
🔹 Our catchment management experts will be on hand to discuss erosion prevention and planting, as well as sustainable land management practices.
🔹 Our Public Transport staff will be available on Friday to provide information related to the Waikato’s bus network and the Te Huia train. 
🔹 Your constituent councillors will be there, so you can chat to them about what’s most important to you.

Learn more here: https://bit.ly/3ReuwGI","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/waikatoregionalcouncil_just-as-it-is-for-many-others-in-the-ag-and-activity-7470366336741814272-ew75"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"Organization","name":"Waikato Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/waikatoregionalcouncil","address":{"type":"PostalAddress","streetAddress":"160 Ward St","addressLocality":"Hamilton Central","addressRegion":"Waikato","postalCode":"3204","addressCountry":"NZ"},"description":"Our people are what makes working here so great.

We have a shared passion for the environment and making the Waikato even better, together, both for the people here today and the generations to come.

We deeply care about our people and are committed to building an organisational culture where we can all be our best. So we’re looking for people who share our values and behaviours:

Kia tika | Responsible
Kia tau | Respectful
Kia toa | Effective.

In our organisation we have many specialists, some who are leaders in their field, so you’re surrounded by people you can learn from. We also invest in training our people, developing their leadership skills and making sure we have a great, flexible working environment.

We offer generous leave entitlements, wellbeing support, and opportunities to develop te ao Māori and te reo Māori capabilities, to name just a few. 

Of course, it helps that our rohe (region) is rich in opportunities for those who love nature – with easy access to east and west coast beaches, hiking and biking trails, as well as rivers and lakes. Our central location puts us close to New Zealand’s largest city, as well as the ski fields. We have a number of offices throughout the mighty Waikato, providing opportunities to work from different locations.

Visit our Careers page to learn more ⬇️

---

Waikato Regional Council takes your privacy seriously.  

We are subject to the Privacy Act 2020 and Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987, which govern how personal information is collected, used, stored and accessed. When we collect information from you, you will be told what we will use it for (unless you have already been informed). Please contact us if you have any questions about our privacy policy, or would like to access or correct your information.

          <p class="break-words text-color-text" data-test-id="about-us__description">
              Our people are what makes working here so great.

We have a shared passion for the environment and making the Waikato even better, together, both for the people here today and the generations to come.

We deeply care about our people and are committed to building an organisational culture where we can all be our best. So we’re looking for people who share our values and behaviours:

Kia tika | Responsible
Kia tau | Respectful
Kia toa | Effective.

In our organisation we have many specialists, some who are leaders in their field, so you’re surrounded by people you can learn from. We also invest in training our people, developing their leadership skills and making sure we have a great, flexible working environment.

We offer generous leave entitlements, wellbeing support, and opportunities to develop te ao Māori and te reo Māori capabilities, to name just a few. 

Of course, it helps that our rohe (region) is rich in opportunities for those who love nature – with easy access to east and west coast beaches, hiking and biking trails, as well as rivers and lakes. Our central location puts us close to New Zealand’s largest city, as well as the ski fields. We have a number of offices throughout the mighty Waikato, providing opportunities to work from different locations.

Visit our Careers page to learn more ⬇️

Waikato Regional Council takes your privacy seriously.  

We are subject to the Privacy Act 2020 and Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987, which govern how personal information is collected, used, stored and accessed. When we collect information from you, you will be told what we will use it for (unless you have already been informed). Please contact us if you have any questions about our privacy policy, or would like to access or correct your information.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">The protection of Coromandel brown kiwi has received a boost with two years of council funding going to conservation group Project Kiwi Trust.

The trust will receive almost $40,000 from Waikato Regional Council’s Environmental Initiatives Fund for the purchase of predator control materials and track maintenance. This represents part of almost $480,000 in grants made to 15 projects announced in the 2025 funding round.

Established in 1996, Project Kiwi Trust works to protect Coromandel brown kiwi on the Kūaotunu Peninsula near Whitianga. For the kiwi population in the area to be stable and experience growth, pest and predator control needs to be maintained.The trust services and checks over 500 traps targeting mustelids throughout the year. They also support a bait station programme that targets rats and possums over some 70ha.

Since 2003, the trust has run a regular kiwi survey. Currently done every two years, the survey sees volunteers deployed to nine base sites over three nights. During a two-hour period each night, they record details about all the bird calls they hear and their location, along with other information such as atmospheric conditions.

Kiwi are also fitted with transmitters, so even though they may not call during the survey, it’s possible to detect them. An additional 17 sites allow for mapping of population change out of the core areas where kiwi have spread. The survey of base sites points to a growing kiwi population estimated at some 300 pairs, plus 150 juveniles and 150 chicks.

Read the full story here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/4vx0xfu?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/4vx0xfu</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Have you thought about pole planting to help erosion control? 

Poplar and willow are ideal to plant on erosion prone hillsides as their extensive root systems bind and hold the soil in place.

Heard that poplar and willow can be a pest? 

There’re a few things to consider. 

Many poplar and willow species and cultivars that were used historically performed well for soil conservation and served their purpose at the time.

However, ongoing research and development have produced improved, smaller-growing varieties with greater resilience, better pest and disease resistance, and fewer management challenges.

Earlier varieties were often more susceptible to disease, more palatable to pests such as possums, tended to grow very large, and were prone to spreading beyond intended areas—via broken branches and twigs (e.g. crack willow), root suckering (e.g. silver poplar), or seeding (particularly female willow varieties).

But today it is possible to select from a short list of varieties with low susceptibility to these problems. 

Purchasing poplar or willow poles, or rooted cuttings from a nursery is recommended to ensure you are purchasing non-invasive varieties that have been specially bred for soil conservation. 

You can find a guide to planting poplar and willow on your property here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/4eAiiVj?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/4eAiiVj</a>

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with MPI and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">We spy a little inanga egg (or two)... 

Our freshwater ecologists in Integrated Catchment Management have been busy undertaking inanga spawning surveys in a tributary of the lower Waikato River. 

While searching monthly from March through to May, they observed an increase in egg density and nest abundances later in the season, along with a greater spatial extent at the site in Port Waikato. This included over 170 eggs in the biggest nest! 

This serves as a good reminder that undertaking multiple surveys across a season is extremely valuable, enabling better management of this newly threatened species within this area. The species has moved from At Risk – Declining to Threatened – Nationally Vulnerable under the Department of Conservations threat classification system. This change is linked to the scarcity of suitable spawning habitat nationwide.

Inanga are native to New Zealand and are the dominant species in the whitebait fishery. They are generally found in lowland systems in the Waikato, as they are poor swimmers and climbers. During the autumn, inanga move downstream to a location called the salt wedge, to catch the new and full moons and the associated spring tides. 

At this time, bankside vegetation is submerged and the inanga spawn hundreds to thousands of eggs amongst it. The eggs develop in the humid air and hatch when they become inundated by the next spring tide in the cycle. The hatchlings are swept to sea where they grow for approximately 20 weeks before returning as whitebait back into our freshwaters.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Have you considered pole planting this winter to help erosion control?

The benefits of planting poplar and willows include:

✅ Root systems which bind more soil than any other tree used on farms
✅ Once established they can reduce slips on hill country by 95%
✅ Sterilised willow also provide significant benefits to river management reducing the erosion of river and stream banks
✅ Well managed space planted poplars and willows allow ~ 90% of pasture growth
✅ Stock utilise their summer shade, and benefit from the shelter
✅ Both species are valuable sources of stock fodder during summer and drought conditions, and pollarding (removing/pruning upper limbs for fodder) helps maintain the canopy while extending the useful life of the trees.
✅ They absorb nutrients, particularly nitrogen from groundwater at deeper levels than pasture and absorb CO2, moderate the temperature and moisture microclimate
✅ They can be managed for timber and wood products and can be tanalised for farm posts, battens and rails 
✅ Increasing farm resilience to severe weather events.

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with MPI and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Do you work with a community biodiversity project in the Waikato region? 

We are currently piloting Kete Taiao Waikato, a new spatial data management tool designed to support community-led biodiversity projects, and we’d love your help. 

Kete Taiao Waikato can be used on desktop or mobile to record things like planting, pest control (animals and plants), monitoring and volunteer hours, all in one place. 

It works in the field and makes it easier to plan activities, track progress, and report on what’s being achieved. 

You can watch a short demo here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/4vGljc0?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/4vGljc0</a> 

We're looking for groups who are:

✅ comfortable using technology (or keen to learn)

✅ willing to actively use the tool and provide feedback

✅ able to put some time into learning and using the system as part of their project work

✅ positive about helping test the tool so it works well for community groups.

If you're interested in being a pilot group for Kete Taiao Waikato, our biodiversity team would like to hear from you. Please email them directly including your group name, a contact person, and a short description of your project to <a class="link" href="mailto:ketetaiao@waikatoregion.govt.nz?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>ketetaiao@waikatoregion.govt.nz</a>.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Waikato Regional Council’s Pathways to the Sea strategy won the Supreme Award at the 2026 LGFA Taituarā Local Government Excellence Awards last night, after winning the category for Excellence in Environmental Leadership.

There were seven categories and 69 entries in total, a record-breaking number of entries celebrating the innovation, leadership and collaboration happening across local government in Aotearoa.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Have you considered pole planting to help erosion control? 

While some highly erosion-prone areas are best retired and planted in natives, others can be managed with pole planting to reduce erosion risk while still supporting productive pasture grazing.

Poplars and willows are valuable assets for any farm, offering strong root systems that contribute to soil retention and the protection of slopes, gullies, streams, and rivers. 

Once established, they can reduce hill country slips by up to 95%, significantly improving land stability. Sterilised willow species also play a crucial role in effective river management by minimizing erosion and helping maintain river channels. 

With thoughtful planting and management, poplars and willows support approximately 90% of pasture growth, ensuring ample grazing for livestock, which also benefit from increased shade and shelter during warmer months. 

Both species are valuable sources of stock fodder during summer and drought conditions, and pollarding (removing/pruning upper limbs for fodder) helps maintain the canopy while extending the useful life of the trees.

Additionally, these trees improve the farm environment by absorbing nutrients from deeper soil layers, particularly nitrogen, and sequestering CO2, resulting in a more resilient microclimate. 

For those interested in timber or wood products, poplars and willows can be managed for farm posts, battens, and rails when treated. 

Collectively, these benefits enhance overall farm resilience, particularly in the face of severe weather conditions.

Landowners in priority catchments may be eligible for up to 70% funding for hill country erosion control work on their property, through our partnership with <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/new-zealand-ministry-for-primary-industries?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI)</a> and the Waikato River Authority.

Want to know more? 

Contact your local Waikato Regional Council catchment management officer on 0800 800 401.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Just as it is for many others in the ag and hospitality sectors, Fieldays is a big deal for us at Waikato Regional Council. 

Months of thinking, planning and organising goes into bringing our site together, with our Communications and Marketing section working closely with teams across our organisation to create a space where landowners, farmers, growers, residents and ratepayers, and industry stakeholders can have meaningful conversations with our people. 

This year our site design brings in two key themes: Our strategic direction and the importance of resilience in the Waikato region.

Taken from Te Pae Tawhiti | Strategic Direction 2026-2036, our map wall celebrates our diverse regional economy spanning agriculture, advanced manufacturing, technology, renewable energy, aquaculture, tourism, healthcare and forestry. You can read our strategic direction here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/43k4esu?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/43k4esu</a>

Building resilience is part of our council’s everyday activities, with environmental, scientific, policy and technical experts working every day managing flood protection infrastructure, generating and making sense of up-to-date data information, protecting and restoring environmental resources, planning transport networks, and so much more. 

We gathered a few of them to share their stories about some of the mahi (work) we are carrying out to support the region and its resilience. You can read them here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/3QfLebs?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/3QfLebs</a>

So, if you’re heading out to Fieldays this week, stop by for a chat. We’ll be at our usual spot inside The Pavilion, site PE 36, with subject-matter experts available to answer your questions.

🔹 Our Primary Industry Engagement team will be on site throughout the week to talk about a range of issues relevant to rural audiences, including farm environment planning.
🔹 Our plant and animal pest team will be there to chat about species you need to look out for as well as tools, tips and support to control pest species around your property.
🔹 Our catchment management experts will be on hand to discuss erosion prevention and planting, as well as sustainable land management practices.
🔹 Our Public Transport staff will be available on Friday to provide information related to the Waikato’s bus network and the Te Huia train. 
🔹 Your constituent councillors will be there, so you can chat to them about what’s most important to you.

Learn more here: <a class="link" href="https://bit.ly/3ReuwGI?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://bit.ly/3ReuwGI</a></p>
